primer.intro: Sorting rearranges a row of values into order, usually smallest to largest. It matters for two reasons. First, many answers are easier to read off a sorted row: the minimum sits at the front, the maximum at the back, duplicates sit next to each other, and the median sits in the middle. Second, sorting unlocks faster tools. Binary search, the sorted two-pointer walks and many greedy proofs only work when the input is ordered, so a single sort often turns a slow nested-loop idea into a fast scan. The simple sorts in this topic - selection, bubble and insertion - each pass over the row many times and cost about n squared steps. The divide-and-conquer sorts - merge and quick - split the row, handle the halves, and combine, costing about n log n steps. You will implement all of them once so that, later, you can call a library sort and still explain what it is doing underneath.
whenToUse: The answer reads naturally off an ordered row: minimum, maximum, median, closest pair or duplicates.
You plan to use binary search, two pointers or a greedy argument that needs order.
The task compares every element with every other element; ordering first often removes a whole loop.
You must arrange records by one field while keeping equal records in their original order - that is a job for a stable sort.
primer.mentalModel: Picture the row split into a sorted part and an unsorted part. Every simple sort grows the sorted part by one element per pass: selection walks the unsorted part to pick its smallest and swaps it to the border; bubble pushes the largest of the unsorted part to its end by neighbour swaps; insertion takes the next element and walks it left into its place. Merge sort thinks differently: halve the row until pieces of one element remain, then zip sorted pieces together. Quick sort picks a pivot, moves smaller values to its left and larger to its right, and recurses on the two sides. When you are stuck, say out loud which part of the row is already sorted and what one more pass adds.
mistakes: Writing the inner loop bounds one step too far and reading past the last index; the sorted border moves every pass, so the bounds must move with it.
Forgetting that bubble sort can stop early: if a full pass makes no swap the row is already sorted, and skipping that check turns a best case of n steps into n squared.
Treating quick sort as always n log n; a sorted input with a poor pivot choice degrades it to n squared, which is exactly why pivot choice is discussed at all.

example.title: Insertion sort, one card at a time
example.explain: The loop invariant is the whole story: before step i, the first i values are sorted among themselves. The next value is lifted out as card, and the while loop shifts every larger neighbour one slot right. The card then drops into the gap. On a nearly sorted row the while loop barely runs, which is why insertion sort is the practical choice for small or almost-ordered inputs.

primer.practice: Ready? Open Practice and implement Selection Sort first - it is the shortest honest sort.

sections.title: Pick the tool by cost and input
sections.text: All five sorts produce the same output, so the choice is about cost and input shape. Selection sort always does the same work - about n squared comparisons - whatever the input looks like, but it writes very little, at most one swap per pass. Bubble and insertion sort reward friendly inputs: on an almost-sorted row they finish in close to n steps. Merge sort guarantees n log n on every input and never degrades, but it pays for that guarantee with a second array during the merge. Quick sort is usually the fastest in practice and sorts in place, yet its worst case is n squared when pivots keep landing on an extreme value. Library sorts hide a hybrid of these ideas; knowing the parts tells you what the hybrid is protecting against.

check.prompt: An input row of one million values arrives almost sorted: each value is at most three slots from its final place. Which tool finishes fastest?

options.explain: It works, but it does the full n log n split-and-merge and ignores the near-order.
Near-sorted input with an extreme pivot is exactly its n squared trap.
Each card walks at most three slots left, so the whole run costs about 3n steps.
It scans the whole unsorted part every pass regardless of order - always about n squared.

check.rereadSectionTitle: Pick the tool by cost and input

reveal.solution: Count the real moves, bit by bit: insertion sort costs one slot-shift per displaced position, and this input promises at most three per element. That linear bound beats every always-n-log-n plan. Selection sort cannot exploit order, and a poor quick-sort pivot is punished by near-sorted rows.

sections.title: Stability, and when it matters
sections.text: A sort is stable when values that compare equal keep their original left-to-right order. Sorting people by age with a stable sort keeps alphabetical order inside each age group if the row was alphabetical first; an unstable sort may shuffle each group. Among the sorts here, bubble, insertion and merge are stable as written, because they only move an element past a strictly larger one. Selection and quick sort are unstable, because a long-distance swap can jump one equal value over another. Stability is the quiet requirement in many interview tasks that say sort by key, then by key two - the clean answer is one stable sort per key, applied from the least important key to the most important.

quiz.prompt: You need the three smallest values of a huge row, and the rest can stay unordered. Which habit from this topic transfers directly?

options.text: Insertion sort of the whole row
options.explain: Also orders everything; the task only needs a tiny ordered prefix.
Three selection passes cost about 3n and deliver exactly the three smallest.

options.text: Full merge sort, then read three values
options.explain: Correct but pays n log n to order values the task never looks at.

options.text: Bubble passes from the left end
options.explain: Bubble pushes maxima to the back; you would need right-to-left passes and care.

quiz.prompt: A task asks you to sort a million records by city, and records of one city must keep their arrival order. What is the key requirement called?

options.explain: That is about exploiting near-sorted input, a different property.
A strategy for speed; it does not by itself preserve arrival order.
Equal keys keep original order - the definition of a stable sort.
That is about extra memory, and says nothing about equal keys.

quiz.prompt: Merge sort and quick sort both split the row. What is the essential difference in where the work happens?

options.text: Merge works while combining halves; quick works while splitting
options.explain: Merge zips two sorted halves; quick partitions around a pivot before recursing.

options.text: Merge uses loops; quick cannot be written with loops
options.explain: Both have loop and recursive forms.
It is the other way around as usually written: merge is the stable one.

options.text: Merge only works on powers of two
options.explain: Any length splits fine; one half is just one element longer.

quiz.prompt: After sorting, which follow-up questions become one linear scan? Pick the best group.

options.explain: Sorting loses original positions; you must record them before sorting.

options.text: Which value appeared first in the input
options.explain: Arrival order is gone after an unstable sort.

options.text: The exact number of swaps bubble sort would make
options.explain: It is a property of the original order - the inversion count - which the sorted output no longer remembers.

options.text: Duplicates, closest pair of values, median
options.explain: Neighbours in a sorted row answer all three in one pass.

quiz.prompt: One bubble pass runs left to right over 5 1 4 2. What does the row look like after that single pass?

options.explain: The 5 keeps moving right past the 2 as well before the pass ends.
Each neighbour swap pushes the 5 rightward until it parks at the end.
That is the fully sorted row; one pass only guarantees the largest is placed.
Compares do happen: 5 beats every neighbour, so swaps occur.

quiz.prompt: Selection sort runs on 3 9 2 8. Which swaps happen, in order?

options.text: 3 swaps with 2, then 9 with 3, then 9 with 8
options.explain: The row walks 2 9 3 8, then 2 3 9 8, then 2 3 8 9 - one swap per pass, three passes.
Selection fills from the front with minima, so the 2 moves first.
Bubble swaps only out-of-order neighbours as it meets them; selection swaps at most once per pass.
The row starts unsorted, so at least the 2 must travel to the front.

quiz.prompt: Merge sort merges the sorted halves 1 4 7 and 2 3 9. Which value is written third?

options.explain: 2 is written second, right after 1.
Writes go 1, 2, then the heads are 4 and 3, so 3 is written third.
4 waits: after 1 and 2, the right head 3 is smaller.
7 is the largest of its half and goes out near the end.

quiz.prompt: Insertion sort on an already sorted row of n values costs about how many comparisons?

options.explain: Every element must at least be visited once, so n is a floor.
Each card compares once with its left neighbour and stays - the adaptive best case.
That is the reversed-input worst case, where every card walks all the way left.
Insertion sort has no halving step to produce a log factor.

quiz.prompt: Which sort keeps the same step count on every input of size n, sorted or shuffled?

options.text: Bubble sort with the early-exit flag
options.explain: The flag lets a sorted input finish after one pass.
Nearly sorted input makes its inner loop almost free.
Its cost swings between n log n and n squared with pivot luck.
It always scans the whole unsorted part to certify each minimum.

quiz.prompt: This bubble pass is wrong. What is the bug?

options.text: The inner loop reads a[j + 1] at j = n - 1, one slot past the end
options.explain: The inner bound must stop at n - 2 (and can shrink by i each pass).

options.text: The outer loop should start at 1
options.explain: Starting at 0 is fine; the pass count is what matters.
Using >= adds pointless swaps of equal values and breaks stability.

options.text: swap is called with the wrong indices
options.explain: Swapping j with j + 1 is exactly the bubble step.

quiz.prompt: This selection sort returns a wrong answer on some inputs. Where is the bug?

options.text: The inner loop must start at i
options.explain: Starting at i + 1 is correct - a[i] is the running candidate already.

options.text: The outer loop must run to n
options.explain: n - 1 passes suffice; the last element is placed by elimination.
j is undefined there; the candidate starts at the border i.

options.text: The swap uses best + 1 instead of best
options.explain: The found minimum sits at index best; shifting by one plants a neighbour instead.

quiz.prompt: Which input exposes the difference between quick sort with a first-element pivot and merge sort most sharply?

options.explain: First-element pivots split 1 against n - 1 every level: n squared versus merge's steady n log n.
Every sort returns it untouched.

options.text: A shuffled row with distinct values
options.explain: Random input is quick sort's happy case.
One comparison either way; both sorts agree.
